How is Virginia divided, and who handles my house?

Virginia has 95 counties and 38 independent cities, which makes 133 local governments in all. Cities sit at the same level as counties, and towns are part of the county around them.

That structure matters when you sell. An independent city is not inside any county, so a house in Richmond, Norfolk or Roanoke is dealt with by the city's own offices. A house in the town of Leesburg or Herndon is dealt with by the county, with the town adding its own rules on top. Fairfax City, for one, is surrounded by Fairfax County yet is politically independent of it.

Under Va. Code 58.1-3310, the commissioner of the revenue keeps the land book, the official property record, and the treasurer gets copies. In practice you will usually talk to two offices:

  • The commissioner of the revenue, for questions about who owns the parcel and how it is listed.
  • The treasurer, for what is owed and how to pay it.

If a guide below lacks a phone number or hours, call the local office before you rely on it. You can also browse every local page through our Virginia guides by city and county.

What does an as-is sale mean in Virginia?

An as-is sale means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and the seller does not fix anything first. Virginia law already leans that way. Under Va. Code 55.1-703, the owner hands the buyer a residential property disclosure statement, and on most topics the owner makes no representations or warranties about the condition of the property.

According to the statute, the topics where the owner makes no representation include:

  • Property condition, covenants and mineral rights
  • Wastewater systems, including septic pump-out costs
  • Radon zones and lead-free plumbing status
  • Whether the property sits in a special flood hazard area

The statute has two versions. The list runs through item 19 until January 1, 2027, and a version effective that date adds an item about use value assessment and possible roll-back taxes. Ask your closing professional which applies to your sale date.

An as-is cash buyer does the inspecting and repair planning on their side, though the disclosure form is still part of the paperwork.

How does foreclosure work in Virginia?

Most Virginia foreclosures run outside the courts. The deed of trust gives a trustee the power to sell, and under Va. Code 55.1-320 the trustee can set the sale at the premises, in front of the circuit court building, or at another place in the county or city where the property lies. Judicial foreclosure is allowed too, but is less common.

Notice rules are spelled out in Va. Code 55.1-321. The timing depends on the kind of property:

RequirementOwner-occupied residentialOther deeds of trust
Certified or registered mail to the ownerNo less than 60 days before saleNo less than 14 days before sale
Ordinary mail to lienholders and certain associationsNo less than 60 daysNo less than 14 days
Subordinate lien recorded before sale75 days30 days

For an owner-occupied home, the owner's notice must carry the statement "This is NOT a notice to vacate the premises" along with a HUD housing counseling website and a statewide legal aid contact. The trustee also needs an affidavit showing the notice went out.

One point surprises many owners. A summary from AllLaw reports that Virginia has no post-sale redemption period. You can redeem before the sale by paying off the whole loan plus fees and costs, and after the sale that door is closed. If you are behind on payments and want to sell, the calendar is short, so talk to a Virginia foreclosure attorney or legal aid office early.

What taxes and fees apply when I sell a Virginia house?

Several costs are set by state law, and others are set by your locality. Here are the ones we could confirm from official pages.

ItemWhat the source says
Recordation tax on a deed (Va. Code 58.1-801)25 cents on every $100 or fraction thereof of the consideration or actual value, whichever is greater
Grantor tax (Va. Code 58.1-802)50 cents for each $500 or fraction thereof; the grantor pays unless the parties agree otherwise
Estate or inheritance tax (Virginia Tax)Virginia no longer has one, though certain remainder interests are still subject to the inheritance tax
Real estate tax due dates (Va. Code 58.1-3916)Set by each locality, in one installment or two
Late interest and penalty caps (Va. Code 58.1-3916)Penalty up to 10 percent of the tax past due; interest generally up to 10 percent a year

If ownership changes after January 1, Va. Code 58.1-3916 says the bill may be reissued to the new owner, with no penalty if it is paid within two weeks after notice is mailed.

Back taxes deserve a closer look. Under Va. Code 58.1-3965, delinquent real estate may be sold in a tax sale, but the owner can redeem at any time before the sale by paying all taxes, penalties, attorney fees, interest and costs. Partial payment is not enough, and a treasurer may suspend a sale under an installment agreement that does not exceed 72 months. See our guides on Virginia tax sales and property tax.

Va. Code 34-4, the homestead statute, protects up to $5,000 of value ($10,000 if the householder is 65 or older), plus up to $50,000 for a principal residence and $500 per dependent, against creditor process. Details are in our homestead exemption guide.

What happens when I inherit a house in Virginia?

Probate starts in a circuit court. Va. Code 64.2-443 gives circuit courts jurisdiction over probating a will, and it sets an order for choosing where: first the county or city where the decedent had a known residence, then the place where real estate owned or devised by the decedent lies, then the place where the person died or had an estate.

If you are unsure which court applies, call the circuit court clerk where your relative lived.

On the tax side, Virginia Tax states that the state no longer has an estate tax or an inheritance tax, with the narrow remainder interest exception noted above. Read our probate guide and our page on the estate and inheritance tax for the next steps.

Can I sell a Virginia house that has tenants?

Yes, though a sale does not erase the tenants' rights. Under Va. Code 55.1-1253, either side can end a month-to-month tenancy with written notice at least 30 days before the next rent due date, unless the agreement says otherwise. A multifamily owner who fails to renew at least 20 month-to-month tenancies, or 50 percent of them, within 30 days must give 60 days' notice to each affected tenant.

We cover the notice types and court steps in our guides to the eviction process and landlord and tenant law.

Who runs the closing, and do I need an attorney?

Someone qualified must run the closing. The State Corporation Commission's settlement agent FAQ says that anyone who conducts the settlement conference and handles money, other than the lender, seller, purchaser or borrower, must be registered. Attorneys admitted to the Virginia State Bar and registered with the Bar do not need to register with the Bureau of Insurance, though an attorney who writes title insurance still needs a title license.

A non-attorney who only conducts settlements must hold a title insurance license and be appointed by a title insurer before registering. Here is what that means for you:

  • Ask the settlement company whether an attorney or a registered agent is handling your file.
  • Ask who holds the deposit and who orders the title search.

Which property issues come up for Virginia sellers?

Radon is one the state tracks directly. The Virginia Department of Health says the EPA sorts radon risk into zones, and that Virginia has 46 counties and 15 cities in Zone 1 (high risk) and 24 counties and 8 cities in Zone 2 (moderate risk). Testing is the only way to know whether a house has a problem.

Flood is another. The disclosure form says the owner makes no representation about special flood hazard areas, and it warns that properties outside those areas can still flood and that standard home insurance generally does not cover flood damage.

The form also points buyers to wastewater systems and septic pump-out costs, so tell any buyer early about a failed system or other known problem.

Where do I look for my own county or city?

Start with the lists below. Each county section links its property tax guide first, then the city pages for places inside it. The independent cities have their own section. If your house is in a town, such as Blacksburg, Leesburg or Herndon, look under the county that contains it.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties does Virginia have?

Virginia has 95 counties and 38 independent cities. Independent cities are not part of any county.

Can I sell my house in Virginia as-is?

Yes. Under Va. Code 55.1-703 the owner gives a disclosure statement, and on most topics makes no representations about condition.

How long does Virginia foreclosure take after notice?

For owner-occupied homes, the notice must be mailed no less than 60 days before the sale under Va. Code 55.1-321. For other deeds of trust the minimum is 14 days.

Can I stop a tax sale?

Yes, by redeeming before the sale. Va. Code 58.1-3965 requires payment of all taxes, penalties, fees, interest and costs.

Does Virginia have an estate tax?

Virginia Tax says it no longer has an estate or inheritance tax, apart from certain remainder interests.

What is the Virginia deed recordation tax?

Va. Code 58.1-801 sets it at 25 cents per $100 of consideration or value, whichever is greater.

Do I need an attorney to close?

Settlement agents must be registered, but registered Virginia State Bar attorneys are exempt from Bureau registration.

How much notice ends a month-to-month lease?

Va. Code 55.1-1253 says at least 30 days before the next rent due date, unless the agreement provides otherwise.
